wajo23_q1.solution:
Let $g, b$ be the value in zogs of green and blue bank notes, respectively. Then
\begin{align*} 3 g+8 b & =46 \tag{1}\\ 8 g+3 b & =31 \tag{2}\\ \therefore(1)+(2): 11 g+11 b & =77 \\ g+b & =7 \tag{3}\\ \therefore(1)-3(3): 5 b & =25 \\ b & =5 \\ \therefore 2 g+3 b & =2(g+b)+b \\ & =2 \cdot 7+5 \\ & =19. \end{align*}
Thus, two green notes and three blue notes are worth 19 zogs.

wajo23_q4.solution:
First observe that $C P D Q$ is a rhombus.
Hence, $C D$ and $P Q$ bisect each other at right angles. So, by Pythagoras' Theorem,
$$ \begin{aligned} P Q & =2 \sqrt{C P^{2}-\left(\frac{1}{2} C D\right)^{2}} \\ & =2 \sqrt{2^{2}-1^{2}} \\ & =2 \sqrt{3} \\ \therefore S & =|C P D Q| \\ & =2|C P Q| \\ & =2 \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot 1 \cdot 2 \sqrt{3} \\ & =2 \sqrt{3} \\ \therefore S^{2} & =12. \end{aligned} $$

wajo23_q6.solution:
Writing $w, d$ and $h$ for the width, depth and height in metres of the box, we have the equations
$$ \begin{aligned} 2(w+d) & =36 \\ 2(w+h) & =38 \\ 2(d+h) & =54 \end{aligned} $$
Halving these equations we have
$$ \begin{aligned} w+d & =18 \\ w+h & =19 \\ d+h & =27 \end{aligned} $$
Half the sum of these last three equations gives
$$ w+d+h=32 $$
so that we get $w=13, d=14$ and $h=5$, and hence the volume is
$$ w d h=13 \cdot 14 \cdot 5=910 \mathrm{~m}^{3} $$

wajo23_q7.solution:
Let $O X=r$. Then $O A=r-9$ and $A B=O C=r-2$. So by Pythagoras' Theorem,
$$ \begin{aligned} O B^{2}=r^{2} & =O A^{2}+A B^{2} \\ & =(r-9)^{2}+(r-2)^{2} \\ & =r^{2}-18 r+81+r^{2}-4 r+4 \\ \therefore 0 & =r^{2}-22 r+85 \\ & =(r-5)(r-17) \\ \therefore r & =17, \text{ since } r>9. \end{aligned} $$

wajo23_q8.solution:
Method 1. We may ignore the number of rounds. Notice the number of participants is 1 more than a multiple of 5, and that each game eliminates 5 participants.
So even the final game has 6 participants.
Therefore, the tournament in eliminating 4320 participants, takes $4320 / 5=864$ games.
Method 2.
Round 1. Since $4321=6 \times 720+1$, there are 720 games and 721 players go to next round.
Round 2. Since $721=6 \times 120+1$, there are 120 games and 121 players go to next round.
Round 3. Since $121=6 \times 20+1$, there are 20 games and 21 players go to next round.
Round 4. Since $21=6 \times 3+3$, ther are 3 games and 6 players go to next round.
Round 5. Since there are 6 players, there is one more game, and the winner of the final game is crowned the winner.
Total number of games is $720+120+20+3+1=864$.

wajo23_q10.solution:
Let $A B C D$ be the trapezium, and let $P, Q, R, S$ be the points at which $A B, B C, C D, D A$, respectively, touch the circle.
By symmetry, $Q, S$ are midpoints of $A D, B C$, respectively.
Let $X$ be the foot of the altitude dropped from $A$ to $B C$ as shown in the diagram.
let $h=A X$ (the height of the trapezium). Then, since tangents from a common point are equal,
$$ \begin{aligned} A P & =A S=\frac{64}{2}=32 \\ & =X Q \\ B P & =B Q=\frac{196}{2}=98 \end{aligned} $$
Method 1. Then,
$$ \begin{aligned} B X & =B Q-X Q \\ & =66 \\ \therefore h & =\sqrt{A B^{2}-B X^{2}} \\ & =\sqrt{(A P+B P)^{2}-B X^{2}} \\ & =\sqrt{130^{2}-66^{2}} \\ & =\sqrt{(130+66)(130-66)} \\ & =\sqrt{64 \cdot 196} \\ & =8 \cdot 14 \\ & =112. \end{aligned} $$
Method 2. Draw a line through $A$ parallel to $D C$ to meet $B C$ at $Y$.
Then $A D C Y$ is a parallelogram.
Our approach is to calculate the area $|A B Y|$ by two methods: "half-base-by-height" and Heron's method. Then,
$$ \begin{aligned} A Y=A B & =A P+B P \\ & =130 \\ B Y & =B C-A D \\ & =132 \\ \therefore s:=\text{ semiperimeter }(A B Y) & =\frac{1}{2}(130+132+130) \\ & =196 \\ \therefore \frac{1}{2} \cdot B Y \cdot h & =\frac{1}{2} \cdot 132 \cdot h \\ & =|A B Y| \\ & =\sqrt{s(s-A B)(s-B Y)(s-A Y)} \\ & =\sqrt{196 \cdot 66 \cdot 64 \cdot 66} \\ & =66 \sqrt{196 \cdot 64} \\ \therefore h & =\sqrt{196 \cdot 64} \\ & =14 \cdot 8 \\ & =112. \end{aligned} $$
Method 3. Let $O$ and $r$ be the centre and radius of the circle, respectively. Since $\angle O S A=90^{\circ}, \angle O A S+\angle A O S=90^{\circ}$. Also,
$$ \begin{aligned} \triangle A S O & \cong \triangle A P O \text{ and } \\ \triangle B P O & \cong \triangle B Q O \\ \therefore \angle B O Q & =\frac{1}{2} \angle P O Q \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\left(180^{\circ}-\angle P O S\right) \\ & =90^{\circ}-\frac{1}{2} \angle P O S \\ & =90^{\circ}-\angle A O S \\ & =\angle O A S \end{aligned} $$
$$ \text{ Also, } \begin{aligned} \angle B Q O & =90^{\circ} \\ & =\angle O S A \\ \triangle B Q O & \sim \triangle O S A, \text{ by AA Rule } \\ \therefore \frac{r}{98}=\frac{Q O}{B Q} & =\frac{S A}{O S}=\frac{32}{r} \\ r^{2} & =32 \cdot 98 \\ & =2^{6} \cdot 7^{2} \\ r & =2^{3} \cdot 7 \\ \therefore h & =2^{4} \cdot 7 \\ & =112 \end{aligned} $$

wajo23_q11.solution:
Call the trains VFT (high-speed train) and ST (slower train).
Let $d$ be the distance from Amble to Bramble,
$v$ be the speed of ST, and
$t$ be the time VFT takes to travel from Amble to Bramble.
Method 1.
VFT travels $d \mathrm{~km}$ at speed $3 v$, while ST travels $(d-320) \mathrm{km}$ at speed $v$, in time $t$. Hence,
$$ \begin{aligned} t=\frac{d}{3 v} & =\frac{d-320}{v} \\ d & =3(d-320) \\ & =3 d-3 \cdot 320 \\ 2 d & =3 \cdot 320 \\ d & =3 \cdot 160 \\ & =480 \mathrm{~km}. \end{aligned} $$
Method 2.
$$ \begin{aligned} v & =\frac{320 \mathrm{~km}}{\left(3+\frac{12}{60}\right) \mathrm{h}} \\ & =\frac{320}{\left(3+\frac{1}{5}\right)} \mathrm{km} / \mathrm{h} \\ & =\frac{320 \cdot 5}{16} \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{h} \\ & =100 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{h} \\ 3 v \cdot t=d & =v t+320 \\ & =\frac{1}{3} d+320 \\ \frac{2}{3} d & =320 \\ d & =\frac{3}{2} \cdot 320 \\ & =480 \mathrm{~km} \end{aligned} $$

wajo23_q13.solution:
Construct diagonal $A C$. Let $P$ be the point where $B F$ and $D E$ intersect. Since $A C$ is an axis of symmetry, $A C$ passes through $P$.
Method 1.
Since triangles $P F D$ and $P C F$ have equal bases $F D$ and $C F$, respectively, relative to a common altitude to $P$,
$$ \begin{align*} |P F D| & =|P F C| \\ & =|P E C|, \text{ since } \triangle P E C \text{ is reflection of } \\ & \hspace{2cm} \triangle P F C \text{ in } P C \\ \therefore |P E C F| & = \frac{2}{3}|D E C| \\ |D E C| & \left.=|A F D|=|A B E|=\frac{1}{4} \right\rvert\, A \\ \therefore|A E P F| & =|A B C D|-|A F D|-\mid A \\ & =204\left(1-\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{4}-\frac{2}{3} \cdot \frac{1}{4}\right) \\ & =204\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{6}\right) \\ & =204 \cdot \frac{1}{3} \\ & =68. \end{align*} $$
Method 2.
For the moment, think of $A B C D$ as a unit square (we will scale later), with $B=(0,0)$ and $E=\left(\frac{1}{2}, 0\right)$.
First we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $P(x, y)$, noting $E D$ is a line of slope 2 passing through $\left(\frac{1}{2}, 0\right)$.
$$ \begin{aligned} B F: y & =\frac{1}{2} x \\ E D: y & =2 x-1, \\ \therefore 3 y & =1, \text{ by } 4 \cdot B F-E D \\ y & =\frac{1}{3} \\ \therefore|A E P F| & =2|A P F| \\ & =2(|A C D|-|A F D|-|F P C|) \\ & =|A B C D|-2(|A D F|+|F P C|) \\ & =1-2\left(\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot 1+\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot y\right) \\ & =1-\frac{1}{2}(1+y) \\ & =1-\frac{1}{2}\left(1+\frac{1}{3}\right) \\ & =1-\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{4}{3} \\ & =\frac{1}{3} \\ \therefore \text{ actual }|A F P E| & =204 \cdot \frac{1}{3} \\ & =68. \end{aligned} $$

wajo23_q14.solution:
Let $r, w, p$ be the numbers of red, white and pink balls, respectively. We are given that the average weight of the red and white balls is $\frac{7}{3} \mathrm{~kg}$. So,
$$ \begin{aligned} \frac{3 r+2 w}{r+w} & =\frac{7}{3} \\ 9 r+6 w & =7 r+7 w \\ \therefore w & =2 r. \end{aligned} $$
The average weight of the red and pink balls is $\frac{10}{7} \mathrm{~kg}$. So,
$$ \begin{aligned} \frac{3 r+p}{r+p} & =\frac{10}{7} \\ 21 r+7 p & =10 r+10 p \\ 11 r & =3 p \\ \therefore p & =\frac{11}{3} r. \end{aligned} $$
And there are 100 balls in all. Thus,
$$ \begin{aligned} 100 & =r+w+p \\ & =r+2 r+\frac{11}{3} r \\ & =\left(1+2+\frac{11}{3}\right) r \\ & =\frac{20}{3} r \\ \therefore r & =\frac{3}{20} \cdot 100 \\ \therefore p & =\frac{11}{3} \cdot \frac{3}{20} \cdot 100 \\ & =55. \end{aligned} $$
So, Mrs Bottleneck has 55 pink balls.

wajo23_q15.solution:
We need a systematic way to construct such strings. Think of there being a gap between each pair of letters. Then among the 40 letters there are 39 gaps. Choosing 2 of these gaps to place boundary markers, e.g.
we have created 3 regions of length at least one, and then we fill the 3 regions with $A \mathrm{~s}$, $B \mathrm{~s}$, and Cs :
$A A A A A A|B B B B B B B B B B B| C C C C C C C C C C C C C C C C C C$
Thus we see that the number of such sequences is the number of ways we can choose to put 2 boundary markers among the 39 gaps, namely,
$$ \binom{39}{2}=\frac{39 \times 38}{2}=741. $$

wajo23_q16.solution:
First note that $8^{m}=\left(2^{m}\right)^{3}$.
Method 1. We rearrange and factorise as follows,
$$ n(n+1)(n+2)=2^{3 m}-2^{9}. $$
Since $n>0$, the left hand side is positive; so $3 m>9$ and the right hand side can be factorised:
$$ n(n+1)(n+2)=2^{9}\left(2^{3 m-9}-1\right). $$
Note the left hand side is a product of 3 consecutive integers, and so is divisible by 3. Therefore $2^{3 m-9}-1$ is divisible by 3, which implies that $3 m-9$ is even. Thus we can factorise the right hand side even further:
$$ n(n+1)(n+2)=2^{9}\left(2^{(3 m-9) / 2}+1\right)\left(2^{(3 m-9) / 2}-1\right). $$
The last two factors differ by 2, and $n, n+2$ differ by 2 ; so let's try,
$$ \begin{aligned} n & =2^{(3 m-9) / 2}-1 \\ n+1 & =2^{9} \\ n+2 & =2^{(3 m-9) / 2}+1. \end{aligned} $$
Then $(3 m-9) / 2=9$, i.e. $m=9$, and $n=2^{9}-1=511$, which works! Since we were given that the problem had a unique solution, $m+n=9+511=520$.
Method 2. We can rewrite the right hand side of the equation as
$$ \begin{aligned} n^{3}+3 n^{2}+2 n+512 & =n^{3}+3 n^{2}+3 n+1+511-n \\ & =(n+1)^{3}+511-n \\ \therefore\left(2^{m}\right)^{3} & =(n+1)^{3}+511-n. \end{aligned} $$
Note also that $n^{3}+3 n^{2}+2 n+512>n^{3}$. Hence, $n>511$ implies $n^{3}<\left(2^{m}\right)^{3}<(n+1)^{3}$, so that $\left(2^{m}\right)^{3}$ would lie strictly between two consecutive cubes, which is impossible.
Therefore, $n \leqslant 511$.
Now observe that $n=511$ yields an integer solution for $m$,
$$ \begin{aligned} \left(2^{m}\right)^{3} & =(n+1)^{3} \\ & =512^{3} \\ & =\left(2^{9}\right)^{3} \\ m & =9. \end{aligned} $$
Since we were given that the problem had a unique solution, $m+n=9+511=520$.
